title: Correlating DC SQUID Performance with the Location of Trapped Magnetic Flux Using Scanning SQUID Microscopy
authors: Bochao Xu, Ian W. Haygood, Kyle Jackman, Coenrad J. Fourie, Pete F. Hopkins, Michael L. Schneider
abstract: Holes in the ground planes of superconducting circuits, commonly referred to as moats, are known to be an effective means of mitigating the deleterious effects of residual magnetic flux in superconducting circuits. Previous studies have utilized scanning SQUID microscopy (SSM) to image the effectiveness of various moat geometries and the maximum magnetic fields where they no longer prevent vortices in the ground plane but have not directly correlated the location of flux with circuit performance measurements. In this study we employ SSM to image the effectiveness of various moat configurations in trapping unwanted flux near a DC SQUID, and when the moats are not effective, the location of vortices in the ground plane. During the same cooldown, and without disturbing the circuit, we measure the circuit performance to directly correlate this with the vortex location. We show that there are preferential pinning sites for fluxons regardless of moat configuration, demonstrating the utility of the SSM in provide feedback for circuit layout, modeling, and failure analysis.
summary: This work uses Scanning SQUID Microscopy (SSM) to image trapped magnetic flux in superconducting circuits while simultaneously measuring the DC SQUID's electrical performance. By correlating the precise location of trapped vortices with changes in the critical current, the authors prove that flux pinning is governed by specific, reproducible physical sites within the multilayer circuit geometry. This provides crucial feedback for designing robust superconducting quantum devices.
main_problem: The study aims to directly correlate the location of trapped magnetic flux (vortices) in the ground plane of superconducting circuits with the measured electrical performance of a DC SQUID.
main_result: The research demonstrates that preferential pinning sites for fluxons exist regardless of moat configuration, providing a powerful tool for validating circuit simulation models and guiding physical layout design.
method: The authors employ Scanning SQUID Microscopy (SSM) to image trapped flux while simultaneously measuring the DC SQUID's critical current ($I_c$) during the same cooldown process.
model_or_system: The physical system is a DC SQUID integrated into a multilayer superconducting circuit featuring engineered ground plane 'moats' designed to mitigate residual magnetic flux.
key_observables: DC SQUID critical current ($I_c$), location and number of trapped fluxons/vortices (visualized by SSM).
important_parameters: Designed zero-field $I_c$ ($\approx 522 \mu	ext{A}$), loop inductance ($L = 9.1 	ext{pH}$), background flux density ($< 1 \mu	ext{T}$).
main_assumptions: The technique assumes that flux trapping can be controlled by cooling in a controlled applied magnetic field, and that the measured $I_c$ can be accurately extracted despite parasitic effects.
figures_summary: Figures show the device structure, the correlation between trapped flux number and measured $I_c$ for multi-moat devices, and simulations illustrating how pinned vortices shift the SQUID's critical current modulation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the methodology of simultaneous SSM imaging and electrical measurement. It then presents detailed results showing how flux trapping affects $I_c$ in multi-moat and single-moat geometries, culminating in a discussion of how local vs. global fields dictate preferred pinning sites.
why_interesting: The direct, simultaneous measurement linking microscopic flux pinning sites (from SSM) to macroscopic device performance ($I_c$) is highly valuable for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in superconducting circuits, which relates to flux quantization and energy landscape mapping.
